newsitem.title: MEXICO: Two dead, 5000 evacuated as Mexico fire rages.
newsitem.headline: Two dead, 5000 evacuated as Mexico fire rages.

text.p: Two people died of their burns on Tuesday and more than 5,000 people were evacuated as firefighters battled an inferno raging for more than a day in three huge fuel tanks that exploded just outside Mexico City.

At least 13 other people were injured, several critically, in Monday afternoon's disaster. Towering columns of flame lit up the Mexico City skyline as thick black smoke billowed three miles (five km) into the air.
State oil monopoly Pemex, which owns the depot where the blast took place, said fireman Jose Luis Romero, 46, and Pemex worker Jose Antonio Ibarra, 34, had died in a hospital of their burns.

The fire flared up again on mid-Tuesday, sparking radio reports that a fourth tank had exploded, but a Pemex official at the scene said a sudden bolt of flame was caused by a collapsing panel on an already burning tank.

Neither Pemex nor the San Juan Ixhautepec district -- known as San Juanico -- are strangers to such disasters. Monday's blast occurred in the same district where a liquefied petroleum gas explosion 12 years ago burned at least 511 people to death and engulfed homes in flames.

Monday's blast occurred when workers from state oil monopoly Pemex were repairing a valve in a tank containing 80,000 barrels of fuel at a storage facility, but the exact cause was not known, Pemex chairman Adrian Lajous said early on Tuesday.
Lajous, Mexico State Gov. Cesar Camacho and other officials denied any other deaths had occurred, although several newspapers claimed up to four firemen were killed.
Opposition politicians called for Lajous to resign and for Pemex's management to be completely overhauled.
"It seems ... maintenance and investment in modernizing equipment just does not happen," said Jalisco state Gov. Alberto Cardenas of the conservative National Action Party (PAN).
"It would seem state firms are black boxes where no one has the right to find out what is being invested in what areas ... and today we are paying the consequences."
The Attorney General's Office said it was setting up a special team of experts to investigate the explosion.

Lajous acknowledged that the blast was the third serious incident involving Pemex in the last two years alone, and more than 200 people died in April 1992 when fuel from a Pemex depot leaked into the Guadalajara sewer system and exploded.

"People don't want to live here anymore; it's not safe," said a 64-year-old San Juanico man who declined to give his name. "Look at all the tanks of gasoline and houses all around. This is a danger zone."
Firefighters trained hoses on flames and other nearby tanks, hoping to stop the blaze from spreading. But the size of the fire continued to dwarf their efforts.
Lajous said he expected the blaze to be extinguished sometime on Tuesday as 100,000 barrels of fuel in the tanks burned off.
The thousands evacuated spent the night in shelters or with relatives; however, some were returning on Tuesday despite the danger, fearing their empty homes would be robbed.

Dozens of dazed firefighters, some struggling to stay on their feet, were treated for smoke inhalation by Red Cross workers. Some complained they lacked proper equipment to fight the massive blaze and had not been fed properly during their round-the-clock shifts.
Lajous said he would set up a special committee to study safety issues urgently because "Mexicans deserve a full explanation."
